title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E449 proves that a prime P has a primitive root a, so that the powers 1, a, a^2, …, a^{Q-1} with Q = P−1 run through all nonzero residues. Earlier sections (§§45–47) showed that a^m is again a primitive root whenever gcd(m,Q) = 1. This gives φ(Q) primitive roots, with the product formula for φ in Coroll. 2.

Scholion 48 (end), the converse: these are all the primitive roots. Every residue equals a^m for some m, because a is primitive. Suppose d = gcd(m,Q) > 1. In the geometric progression 1, a^m, a^{2m}, … the term with exponent (Q/d)·m appears before a^{Qm}. That exponent also equals (m/d)·Q, a multiple of Q, so this term already leaves residue 1. Hence the period of a^m is at most Q/d < Q, the residue series is incomplete, and a^m is not a primitive root. In modern terms: ord(a^m) = Q/gcd(m,Q), so the primitive roots are exactly the a^m with gcd(m,Q) = 1, and there are φ(P−1) of them.

Coroll. 4 (§49): write P = 2n+1, so Q = 2n. If r ≡ a^{n−λ}, its 'socius' s comes from a^{n+λ}. Since a^{n−λ}·a^{n+λ} = a^{2n} ≡ 1, the socius is the multiplicative inverse of r mod P. Because (n−λ) + (n+λ) = 2n = Q, the two exponents are simultaneously coprime to Q. So the inverse of a primitive root is again a primitive root.

Scholion 50 introduces the table on the next page. It lists, for each prime P ≤ 37, the exponents prime to P−1 and the corresponding primitive roots.
errors: No mathematical errors. Minor gap in Coroll. 4: Euler does not separately note the case λ = 0 (r = s = a^n ≡ −1). It is harmless, because n is coprime to 2n only when n = 1 (P = 3), where −1 = 2 is indeed the primitive root.

ideas.what: If gcd(m,P−1) = d > 1, then a^m has period dividing (P−1)/d, so it is not a primitive root; hence the primitive roots are exactly a^m with gcd(m,P−1) = 1, and there are φ(P−1) of them.
ideas.modern_name: Order of a power in a cyclic group: ord(g^m) = n/gcd(m,n); the number of generators is φ(n)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E449, 1774) for the count of primitive roots; Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), art. 52–55, for systematic treatment
ideas.where_published: E449 itself, §§45–48; anticipated in E262 (Theoremata circa residua ex divisione potestatum relicta)

ideas.what: The 'socius' (multiplicative inverse) of a primitive root is a primitive root, since exponents n−λ and n+λ sum to P−1.
ideas.modern_name: The inverse of a generator of a cyclic group is a generator

ideas.what: Plan to tabulate primitive roots for small primes, indexed by exponents coprime to P−1.
ideas.modern_name: Tables of primitive roots and indices (precursor of Jacobi's Canon Arithmeticus, 1839)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E449 table); Gauss DA table; Jacobi 1839

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard elementary facts about cyclic groups. They are well known to be in E449, which is the classic, much-discussed source for Euler's (incomplete) primitive-root proof and his table of primitive roots.
